newsitem.title: UK: Dollar hugs lower levels in Europe, eyes jobs data.
newsitem.headline: Dollar hugs lower levels in Europe, eyes jobs data.

text.p: The dollar traded near session lows at midday in Europe, but ranges were uninspiring as the market held fire before Friday's key U.S. payrolls data.
Dollar/yen was down more than half a yen from Wednesday's close here, undermined by healthy trade surplus figures from Japan and Bank of Japan talk of pre-emptive monetary policy.
Dollar/mark, meantime, was supported by nagging uncertainty over European monetary union and fears of a large increase in German unemployment in May figures due out on Friday.
German newspaper Berliner Zeitung, citing official data, said seasonally-adjusted jobless had risen by 60,000.
"We're stuck in a range until payrolls," said Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ International in London.

But the breakout could come if the payrolls come in strong. With many economists' forecasts revised down after seasonal adjustments by the U.S. Labor Department, analysts said the risk was for higher-than-expected payrolls -- and a firmer dollar.
"The combination of a big rise in German unemployment and a strong payrolls number could well push the dollar up towards the year's highs," Edmonds said.
The dollar was trading at 1.7266/71 marks and 115.60/70 yen at 1049 GMT versus 1.7305/13 and 116.22/32 late Wednesday.
The U.S. currency touched a four-week high of 1.7340 marks intraday on Wednesday, setting the market's sights on its 1997 peak of 1.7389.
"I think the dollar is poised for a leap forward. It could get up to 1.75 in June without any problem at all," said Stuart Frost, market analyst at Natwest Markets here.
"With the turmoil going on in Europe, the market is looking for safe havens and those include the dollar, the Swiss franc, sterling, and even the yen is making a comeback," he added.
Though the row between Bonn and the Bundesbank over asset revaluation has been settled, EMU tensions are still simmering.
Germany's government and central bank agreed the transfer of funds from asset revaluation would not commence until 1998. The decision on who will found EMU will be based on 1997 data.

That, plus the prospect of a sharp increase in May unemployment, has rekindled fears Germany will miss EMU entry goals, though Finance Minister Theo Waigel insisted on Thursday that Germany would do its utmost to meet the criteria.
Waigel also said talk now of EMU delay would be wrong.
Concerns that monetary union would be postponed or engender a weak currency were fanned at the weekend when the left wing swept to power in France's parliamentary election.
EMU delay is usually seen as mark-positive, as the market anticipates a flight into the hard core of Europe and a reduced risk of the mark being subsumed into a weaker common currency.

But the French Socialists have declared their commitment to the euro timetable, and their drive for Italy and Spain to join in the first wave of EMU in 1999 has pushed market expectations towards a broad, weak euro rather than a delayed launch.

While all this is supportive for dollar/mark, the outlook is not so rosy for dollar/yen, analysts said. Data released overnight showed Japan recorded a 41.16 billion yen surplus for the first 20 days of May.

"The trade surplus is still going up and will continue to go up. That's the strongest factor supporting the yen, but also the view that Japanese rates are going up at some stage is going to return to the market," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
The rate-hike fever which swept the market last month has cooled lately. But BOJ governor Yasuo Matsushita said overnight the bank was ready to act pre-emptively on monetary policy.
The firmer yen saw mark/yen fall to 66.92/94 by 1136 GMT from 67.14/17 in late Europe on Thursday.
-- Abigail Levene, London Newsroom +44-171-542-8968
